reference_opening.argument: This video is non-scam content because it presents an interview and educational discussion of STRC, including how the product works, its Bitcoin exposure, tax treatment, and potential risks. The speakers discuss possible losses, Bitcoin volatility, leverage, and criticism that the product could be a Ponzi scheme rather than concealing those issues. Although the title and description highlight the yield and include promotional links, the material does not establish a deceptive solicitation with a guaranteed outcome or a specified money or data transfer to the creator.

opening.argument: Judge the return claim together with the action it encourages. The guest says the product pays an 11.5% dividend monthly, then tells a yield-seeking investor, “I would just buy it and hold it.” The description also provides a “More Info” link for STRC, while the displayed product page places its dividend rate beside a brokerage purchase button. That is a participation pathway, not merely an abstract discussion of yield. The interview supplies a reason to buy, a suggested holding strategy, and a route toward purchase.

rebuttal.rebuttal: An interview format and an explanation of preferred equity do not erase the guest’s purchase recommendation. The defense cites a severe Bitcoin-loss scenario, but that caveat does not change the direction of the advice to a yield-seeking viewer. Nor does the absence of a payment to the creator settle whether viewers are being steered to purchase the featured product: the displayed brokerage button supplies a route to do so.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The cited material shows promotion of an investment, not deception. The guest identifies it as preferred equity and explains that the dividend depends on a strategy exposed to Bitcoin; he also names a scenario in which a prolonged price collapse would be a problem. A brokerage purchase button and an information link provide ways to investigate or buy a disclosed product, but neither establishes a false promise or concealed transfer.

opening.argument: The warning signs reinforce one another. The title leads with an “Insane 11.50% Cash Yields” claim; the guest describes taking on Bitcoin volatility while giving the customer much lower volatility; and the interview offers a tactic of buying before a record date, selling the next day, and getting paid. The host even raises whether the offer sounds too good to be true. Together, these claims present a strikingly easy route to high income. The judge should give particular weight to how that impression could affect a viewer deciding whether to buy.

We strip that away and we give to the end customer 2% vol.
you want to buy the product on the 14th and then you want to sell it on the 15th hold it for one day get paid 11 and a half percent

rebuttal.rebuttal: The defense is right that Bitcoin downside is mentioned. But its quoted warning is conditional, whereas the buy-and-sell example gives a concrete next-day action tied to payment. Explaining volatility does not necessarily undo the impression created by pairing a high advertised yield with an apparently simple way to collect it. The issue is the combined message, not whether any single sentence guarantees an outcome.

you want to buy the product on the 14th and then you want to sell it on the 15th hold it for one day get paid 11 and a half percent

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The one-day passage describes trader behavior around a monthly record date; it does not establish an 11.5% return earned in one day. The guest also calls the product preferred equity, discusses its Bitcoin exposure, and identifies both leverage and a sustained Bitcoin decline as risks. Strong promotional language may warrant skepticism, but these quotes do not show that the yield or purchase mechanics are fabricated.

opening.argument: The interview’s educational framing should not obscure its promotional function. The host praises the company’s innovation, the guest calls the product “the best of both worlds,” and the description directs viewers to more STRC information. The displayed product page includes a brokerage purchase button. Even the discussion of criticism gives the product’s creator room to answer the Ponzi concern himself. Taken together, the segment does more than explain an investment: it builds confidence in it and moves an interested viewer toward buying.

citations.quote: Kudos to you guys for that.
What we brought is the best of both worlds. High yields, tax deferral, plus short duration.
GUEST: Phong Le, CEO at Strategy $STRC More Info ➜ https://bit.ly/btcSTRC

rebuttal.rebuttal: Calling the segment education does not make its praise neutral. The defense points to the host raising a Ponzi criticism, but the response is delivered by someone who says he helped create and back the product. That exchange lets the promoter address an objection within the same segment that praises the product and directs viewers to further STRC information. The criticism’s presence therefore does not, by itself, resolve the concern about promotional framing.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: A favorable interview can still be financial discussion rather than a scam. Here the host explicitly challenges whether the product is too good to be true, and the guest describes both the proposed use of purchase proceeds and the issuance of common equity to pay dividends. Those explanations are claims to assess, not independent verification; equally, praise, an information link, and a purchase button do not establish that viewers are being deceived.
